text:
Text of New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie’s 2014 State of the State address as prepared for delivery Tuesday:
Lt. Governor, Mr. Speaker, Mr. President, Legislators, friends, fellow New Jerseyans:
The last week has certainly tested this Administration. Mistakes were clearly made. And as a result, we let down the people we are entrusted to serve. I know our citizens deserve better. Much better.
I am the governor and I am ultimately responsible for all that happens on my watch – both good and bad.
Without a doubt we will cooperate with all appropriate inquiries to ensure this breach of trust does not happen again.
But I also want to assure the people of New Jersey today that what has occurred does not define us or our state. This Administration and this Legislature will not allow the work that needs to be done to improve the people’s lives in New Jersey to be delayed. I am the leader of this state and its people and I stand here today proud to be both. And always determined to do better.
Now I come before you once again to report on the state of our state.
And today, the state of the state is good, and getting better.
Four years ago, we were in the throes of economic crisis. Today, our unemployment rate is 7.8 percent, the lowest in 5 years.
Four years ago, we were losing jobs. Today, we have gained 70,000 jobs in the last year alone, and a total of 156,000 in the last four years.
Four years ago, wealth and jobs were leaving the state. Today, personal income for New Jerseyans is at an all-time high, and we are attracting new companies.
And that has brought jobs – four straight years of private sector job growth. In fact, in November, the drop in our unemployment rate was the largest one month drop ever measured. And in the last year, New Jersey had the second largest drop in its unemployment rate in America.
We could have chosen to go down a path of continued tax increases to fund the state’s addiction to spending.
But we didn’t. We held the line against any new taxes, and brought spending in the current fiscal year to a level below Fiscal 2008 – six years ago.
We could have let state government grow, even while the private sector shrank. But we didn’t. Today, there are 6,000 fewer state employees than four years ago, but over 155,000 more private sector employees.
We improved our business climate, and today, by every measure, business confidence in New Jersey is up. In fact, one national magazine ranked New Jersey among the top 5 states with the most improved business climates in America.
It’s no accident how we got to this place today. We chose the way. And in this new year and in the next four years, we need to build on this momentum by creating a new attitude: we need to create an attitude of choice.
It is not about choosing everything; it is not about saying yes to everyone; it is about setting our priorities and choosing to invest in New Jersey where it matters and to put in place the reforms and reductions that make it possible.
And the best part of our turnaround in these past four years is because we have chosen to work together. These are our achievements.
Four balanced budgets. Passed with bipartisan support. Pension reform and tenure reform. Passed with bipartisan support. A cap on property taxes. Passed with bipartisan support.
We acted and we acted together.
Even though the competition among the states is fierce, no state has shown more bipartisan cooperation over the last four years than New Jersey. Let’s do it again. Let’s resolve that in spite of politics, we will continue to put our people first. We will choose to do our jobs.
One of the things that drove people out of New Jersey in the past decade was high property taxes. In 2010, together, we capped them. The 2 percent cap has worked. In these past two years, property tax growth has been the lowest in two decades.
But the job is not finished. Property taxes are still too high. So today, I ask for you to join me in enacting a new property tax relief initiative that tackles the root causes that are driving up property taxes in the first place.
First, some context: the 2 percent cap we’ve already enacted has worked for a reason. We’ve done it by controlling costs. We accompanied it with reform of an interest arbitration award system that needed fixing.
As you know, the interest arbitration cap was not permanent – it is set to expire this April, unless we act. So I ask you today, let us renew the cap on interest arbitration awards and make the cap permanent.
Another reason property taxes are so high is that our cities and towns are stuck with a series of costly state rules that increase the cost of local government. As the cost of government grows, taxpayers are paying the price.
We have worked with the Senate to try to pass real consolidation and civil service reform. We haven’t gotten it done in the Assembly. We need to have an effort that includes everyone responsible for property taxes – the Senate, the Assembly, our Administration and local government to provide local government with the authority to run their governments like a business: consolidate, share services, cut duplication and ultimately actually reduce property taxes.
Look at what happened last year in Princeton. Princeton Borough and Princeton Township consolidated into a single government. Not two tax departments, two police forces, two offices answering the phone. The savings in one year: $3 million. That’s on a budget of $64 million, a 4.7 percent savings. And the citizens of Princeton got this: more services, despite a smaller budget, and a reduction in municipal taxes.
This is not just my opinion – the local unit alignment, reorganization and consolidation commission said that civil service seniority rules were at the top of the list of barriers to shared services. Let’s help our towns clear away arcane rules that stand between them and lower property taxes.
When it comes to driving costs, let’s not forget the expensive practice of sick leave payouts for government employees. Sick time should be used when you’re sick. If you’re lucky enough to be healthy, that’s your reward. Sick leave has been abused too many times, and the cost is real. Almost a billion dollars in liability facing New Jersey towns – $880 million to be exact. And it will only get higher if the system is not fixed. These reforms are common sense: let’s lift this billion dollar albatross off the necks of New Jersey’s towns. Let’s together enact the zero means zero plan.
Our pension system is burdened by some who collect disability retirement because they claim they are “totally and permanently disabled,” but who are now working full-time. So we’ve established by Executive Order a special unit to prosecute pension fraud. Let’s go even further to solidify our pension system and reduce costs by reforming our disability retirement system to end this fraud and abuse. This will also help us to reduce property taxes.
And some towns get around the property tax cap by enacting user fees to fund traditional services that used to be in the budget. Let’s end this practice.
I will have more to say about New Jersey’s taxes when I present my budget to you next month. That is for a reason. We have to consider changes to our tax system in the context of our overall budget picture. We will present some of these choices in February.
I will tell you one choice we will not make – because it is one answer that will not help grow our state: raising taxes.
If the evidence is clear that increasing taxes hurts our growth, it is equally clear that improving education is a key to helping our growth.
We’ve made some great progress in these past four years: a record amount of school aid, long-overdue reform of our system of teacher tenure, an increase in the number of charter schools and an Urban Hope Act that is bringing renaissance schools to some of our most challenged cities.
Some results are promising too. Last year, New Jersey’s high school graduation rate increased by a full percentage point, to 87.5 percent. Student achievement is strong in many of our public schools, and New Jersey’s students are among the country’s greatest achievers. Just a few years ago, a graduate of my own high school, Livingston High School, won the Nobel Prize in chemistry.
We are making a large investment in public education: New Jersey spends over $25 billion a year, all told. Our per pupil expenditure is the highest in the nation at over $17,000 per year.
In some cases – too many – our children are not receiving the education they deserve. While many public schools are strong, too many are still failing. While the vast majority of teachers are performing well, some are underperforming – and they should be removed from the classroom.
The need to be better is particularly acute in New Jersey’s cities. Our urban schools demand our attention, and believe me, they have mine.
Where bold action was necessary, we have taken bold action. And we have made a commitment to the kids in our cities that they have a right to the same quality education as kids in our suburbs.
In our largest school system, in Newark, we have brought in a new organization and new resources, not only in the form of state aid but in collaboration with parents, teachers, and community leaders on the ground. One result – we negotiated a historic contract with the teacher’s union and delivered real merit pay alongside increased teacher involvement.
Most importantly we want to encourage innovation while listening to the specific needs of our urban communities. It’s the reason why we have empowered our superintendents in Newark and Camden to make choices that work best for their kids, their parents and their schools.
In Newark, that superintendent is Cami Anderson.
Cami has moved to pay the best teachers, to stop actions that are failing kids, to empower 50 new principals, create cooperation between public schools and charter schools and reorganize the school systems’ structure to focus on putting students, schools and parents first.
Early childhood enrollment has increased by more than 1,000 students. Graduation rates have increased by 10 percent.
Newark is leading the conversation in making sure every kid – those who are behind, those who are ahead, those who have special education needs – are lifted up.
Every kid means every kid.
Her efforts haven’t always been met without skepticism, but she is a true partner with Newark. Cami is here with us today – Cami, thank you for your commitment to our kids.
How bad has it been in Camden? Last year, only three students graduated “college ready.” Paymon Rouhanifard is bringing that same energy to Camden’s public schools. He has turned around a perennially low-performing charter school to showing some of the largest academic gains in the state. He has launched a new “safe corridors” program with Mayor Dana Redd, which has created safe walking routes to and from school for our children.
And, of the 345 students who have dropped out in the last year, we went door-to-door and re-enrolled 50 of them.
Paymon, thank you for your efforts and your dedication.
Both Cami and Paymon have this Administration’s confidence and support to continue the aggressive reforms needed that work best for the communities of Newark and Camden and put kids first.
Cami and Paymon are emblems of my commitment to ensuring the opportunity for an excellent education to every child in New Jersey, regardless of the zip code.
Despite the improvements we are seeing in Newark and Camden, I believe we need to take bigger and broader steps to adjust our approach to K-12 education to address the new competitive world we live in. Our school calendar is antiquated both educationally and culturally. Life in 2014 demands something more for our students. It is time to lengthen both the school day and school year in New Jersey.
If student achievement is lagging at the exact moment when we need improvement more than ever in order to compete in the world economy, we should take these steps – every possible step – to boost student achievement.
And one key step is to lengthen the school day and the school year. So, working with Commissioner Cerf, I will present to you shortly a proposal to increase the length of both the school day and the school year in New Jersey. This is a key step to improve student outcomes and boost our competitiveness. We should do it now.
Many of our new initiatives recognize a core feature of modern American life: that the quality of education and the quality of life in our communities are inextricably intertwined.
That is why this year, we need to be more aggressive, and bolder, in fixing our failing schools – and delivering a choice to those for whom today the only option is a bad option: a failing school.
This is a moral obligation. We must give every New Jersey child the chance to graduate from high school, to be ready for college and to prepare for a career. If we fail to meet this obligation, we compromise the life of that child, and we hurt the quality of life in our communities and in New Jersey. So failure is not an option.
If education is one key to the quality of life in New Jersey communities, our approach to safe streets and stronger communities is another.
Every New Jerseyan should be concerned when violent crimes occur right before our eyes.
Last month, a young lawyer went to open the door of his car for his wife after an evening of pre-Christmas shopping. He was set upon by thugs who wanted to car-jack his S.U.V. and, in front of his new wife, he was shot in the head and left for dead on the deck of the mall parking garage.
Outstanding police work led to four arrests, and the suspects are now charged with murder.
All four had prior criminal records. All four are, fortunately, now in jail.
How can we tolerate such violence in our midst? The answer is obvious: we cannot.
We must take a new approach to fighting crime in New Jersey and prevent tragedies like this from happening. We must do everything we can to swiftly jail those violent criminals who bring additional murder and disruption to innocent victims across our state. We have the tools to do this – some we’ve begun, some we have not. 2014 must be the year we finish the job.
What have we not finished? Almost two years ago, I announced a proposed constitutional amendment to modify the right to bail in New Jersey.
The concept is simple: New Jersey courts should have the right to keep dangerous criminals off the streets and in jail until trial.
Why is this important? A study by the federal government’s Justice Department found that one-third of defendants released before trial ended up being charged with some type of pre-trial misconduct. One-sixth were arrested for a new offense – and half of those were felonies.
The federal government allows a violent criminal who is a danger to the community to be held without bail. New Jersey law does not. This must change. How can we justify exposing our citizens to the risk of violent crime at the hands of those, already in custody, who we know are disposed to commit it? There is no justification for that. Let us mirror federal law. Pass bail reform now.
In the past few years, we have made progress in reducing crime in New Jersey. Over the past decade, violent crime is down 16percent, both across New Jersey, and in our 15 largest urban centers. And the state’s prison population is down 20percent since 1999.
But we can do better, and we must. Those 15 urban centers still account for more than half of all the violent crime in New Jersey, despite representing only 18percent of the state’s population.
For too long, Camden has been one of the most dangerous cities in New Jersey, and in America.
The ability to put police on the street was constrained by tight budgets, low morale, and an absentee rate that sometimes reached 30 percent.
Under an agreement that this Administration signed with the City of Camden and Camden County, we have regionalized the police force. A police force of slightly more than 200 that was sharply reduced in response to budget cuts is now being beefed up to 400 county police officers.
Last year, the homicide rate was down, and the crime rate was down – by over 20 percent.
The battle is far from won. But under Mayor Dana Redd, Police Chief Scott Thomson, and Jose Cordero, who helped decrease crime in East Orange by 75 percent, Camden is using a new approach – using technology to predict crime, and engaging the community.
Camden is moving in the right direction. And I agree with Senator Sweeney that we should have incentives for other communities to adopt the shared service agreements and regional police forces that are making more cops on the street possible. More cops on the streets means safer communities. To make this happen, we will reintroduce shared services and consolidation reform in this session of the Legislature.
We must reach out a hand of compassion and common sense to those who commit non-violent crimes. We must do a better job of reclaiming their lives and putting them back on the road to success and engagement with society. My belief is simple: every human life is precious, and no life is disposable.
That is why I proposed last year to change our approach to non-violent drug offenders, and mandate treatment, not imprisonment. Together, we made this possible.
The drug court program has been a success, thanks in part to your support in funding both the court and the treatment.
And I thank you for passage this past year of the Overdose Protection Act. We should not be prosecuting those Good Samaritans and health professionals who are trying to help in a life-threatening overdose situation.
New Jersey’s approach to reclaiming lives is working. Recidivism has dropped by 11 percent, one of the steepest drops in America. And New Jersey is rightly recognized by national experts as a leader among states in reducing incidents of recidivism.
For me this is personal. In this room today is a man who was a drug addict at 16 years old. His life was at risk, but treatment saved him. He was rehabilitated at Daytop Village. He graduated from high school, went to college, and ultimately got a law degree. I had the privilege of hiring and working with Craig Hanlon at the U.S. Attorney’s Office, and Craig is with us now in this Chamber. If you need proof that reclaiming a life is possible and that every life has precious value, then that proof is standing before you today. Craig, welcome – and thank you for making new jersey a better place.
Because of Craig, I know the passion and strength that comes from the desire to have a better life. And I believe we can do more to help give people a second chance. That is why I am proposing an initiative to expand integrated treatment and employment services for individuals receiving drug treatment services.
By providing grant funds in the amount of $500,000 to be managed in partnership with The Nicholson Foundation, we will place individuals in jobs and help improve their retention. We will work directly with treatment providers to integrate employment services with treatment services for drug court participants.
Research shows that employment during substance abuse treatment helps ensure continued participation in treatment and sustainable long-term employment. With this partnership we will help empower individuals who want and deserve the opportunity to live a life well lived.
A year ago this afternoon, our state was in recovery from a challenge not of our own making.
Superstorm Sandy devastated New Jersey in the fall of 2012 – flooding our homes, turning off our power and destroying our roads. Despite the magnitude and devastation of the storm, Sandy could not break out spirit.
This past summer, most businesses at the Shore opened on time. Boardwalks were rebuilt. The crowds came back. And schools that had been damaged were re-opened.
Today, about nine months after the first phase of CDBG disaster recovery funds started flowing in New Jersey, nearly $900 million – more than two-thirds of the funds for housing recovery programs are out the door or in the pipeline.
From the very beginning, the priority was putting those with the greatest needs and with the most limited financial resources at the front of the line. Of the nearly half of the housing money that has been obligated so far, 72.9 percent has been awarded to low- and middle-income families.
The bottom line is this: we are a long way from the finish line, but we are a long way from where we were one year ago. Challenges remain and I will not rest until every person hurt by Sandy has their life back. That is my mission.
I want to thank this Legislature, and all New Jerseyans, for the cooperative, bipartisan and resilient spirit you demonstrated in coming back from Sandy. Let that spirit of Sandy be a powerful lesson to all of us, that when times are most difficult, cooperation and progress are possible. Indeed, they are necessary.
Lastly, let me share with you one more, hard truth that makes this new attitude of choice necessary for New Jersey’s future.
We have discussed many exciting opportunities for investment in our state. K-12 education. Higher education. Crime prevention. Drug rehabilitation and job training. Health care. Infrastructure investment. Lower taxes. Job growth. All exciting, all of which, done responsibly, could make New Jersey an even greater place. But here is the simple truth. We cannot afford to do it right now.
Why?
Because of our pension and debt service costs. For the Fiscal Year 2015 Budget, the increase in pension and debt service costs could amount to as much as nearly $1 billion.
That’s nearly $1 billion we can’t spend on education. That we can’t invest in infrastructure improvement. That we can’t use to put more cops on the street. That won’t be available to improve access to health care. And for those who would advocate for higher income taxes like the ones I have vetoed before, remember that the amount raised would not even cover the increase in our scheduled pension payment and would undoubtedly make us less competitive in the job market nationwide.
These are the consequences of failing to engage in an attitude of choice. If we continue in an era where we believe we can choose everything, we are really choosing nothing. We need to have the conversation now about further changes to our pension system and to adding further to the state’s debt load. But the time to avoid this conversation and these choices is nearly over.
If we do not choose to reduce our soaring pension and debt service costs, we will miss the opportunity to improve the lives of every New Jersey citizen, not just a select few.
I am ready to engage in those conversations and help, with you, to truly create an attitude of choice. The result will be a better, smarter, stronger New Jersey. The results from our refusal to choose – a weaker New Jersey with a middle class burdened by even higher taxes. That is an abandonment of our duty.
Centuries ago, a philosopher wrote that “choice, not chance, determines your destiny.” And this remains true for New Jersey today.
Our destiny is not set – it is the product of the choices we make. Our future is not set – it, too, is the product of the choices we make from this day forward.
So let us choose wisely. And let us not fail to act. Let us create an attitude of choice.
Let us choose to invest in better schools, and not a status quo in which we leave some children behind and put the rest at risk of being swallowed by a rising tide of mediocrity.
Let us choose the path of safer streets, and not leave our families vulnerable to the heartless carjackers and muggers who would destroy our quality of life.
Let us celebrate every life by creating an opportunity for every citizen, through an excellent education, a productive job, and a thriving community.
In this hour of choice, let us choose a better New Jersey. For that is what we owe our citizens, our children, and ourselves.
New Jersey has long been blessed by an abundance of natural resources and human talent. In 2014, we have been blessed by a return to prosperity.
Let us all choose to make the most of it – together.
Thank you, God bless you, and God bless the great state of New Jersey.

I’m thrilled to be back up here and I can't thank you all enough for coming out today, and not just for that but for all the work that you've been doing for me during this campaign. I get the numbers every week and watch what is being done up here in Sussex County, the phone calls, the door knocks, all the incredible work that you’re doing. So, on behalf of me and Mary Pat, who is doing hockey and basketball this afternoon, I just can't thank you enough for what you're doing. So, we've got three days to go. Three days to go and I want to tell you that for me the thing I'm worried about the most with three days to go. We have got great poll numbers; we all love that, we love being ahead rather than being behind and it feels really good, but we know that nothing's won until Tuesday night at eight o’clock. And so, our biggest concern between now and Tuesday at eight o’clock is complacency. I'll give you one example. I was at the Empire Diner in Parsippany two mornings ago and a woman came up to me and said to me, “Governor, I really love the job you're doing. I'm a huge supporter and I can't wait to vote for you for president.” And I said, “Well that's very nice but you know I have an election coming up on Tuesday that you could consider voting in.” And she said, “Oh, you got it wrapped up.” No, no. We can’t have that, especially in places like Sussex county, in Warren county, in Morris county, the bedrock of our Republican party.
So, for the next three days if you're making phone calls and knocking on doors, I say thank you. I really appreciate it and I can't thank you  enough. And if you're not one of those people who are doing that, there's still things you can do. You can make sure that you talk to your neighbors and your friends, that you talk to your relatives and your co-workers. In the next three days you are really important for the folks that you see in the supermarket checkout line or the folks you see as you pick up your kids from school. If you have some of those stickers on, why don’t you keep them on, you know, and then look and say I was with the governor, I’ve met him before, I’ve looked him in the eye, I've taken the measure of his record and what he's done, and I'm working for him helping him, and I want you to vote for him. I can tell you that's the most powerful thing in politics today. It's more powerful that the 30-second ad is, more powerful than a piece of mail in the mailbox. It is definitely more powerful than those annoying automated phone calls you're getting. More powerful than all those things is neighbor to neighbor contact: you speaking to people that know you and trust you and know you're involved and you tell them I'll not only vote for the governor, I'm working for him. That's powerful. That's powerful and that's what we need to do over the next three days because we do not want to go back to what the state was like four years ago.
You know, we've got all the great representatives that you have not only in your county government but the legislators who you sent down to Trenton from here are extraordinary. They are great supporters of mine and they deserve your support. The entire Republican ticket. Don't even bother looking someplace else. Just go across the entire Republican ticket and you’ve got my word that they’re good people.
{shouting from audience}
All of you need to understand that we have a challenge on our hands, a challenge to take our state back from people like that. That’s what our challenge is: to bring common sense back to government, is to bring conservative values back to government so that every day that we’re working to empower you and your families to be able to keep more of your own money. If you give me a Republican legislature in three days, I'm going to cut taxes in the first week of my new term. And we will continue to fight as we have fought against the taking of lands up here to the highlands. And if you give me a Republican legislature we’re going to change that too.
So, there are things that absolutely need to be done in this state to make us more competitive, to help create more jobs, put more people back to work where they belong in the private sector not in the public sector. We are proud of the fact that the government is 5,200 jobs smaller than when I took it over four years ago at the state level and 25,000 fewer government jobs at every level of government. We're setting the tone at the top. Give money away from the government and give it back to you for all of you to
invest in the businesses that you want to invest in.
I will tell you that there are the forces that will always fight against us. You're seeing it on TV every day:  the folks who believe that the government and your tax dollars are their personal piggy bank to play with and to socially engineer. We've got to send a strong message in the last three days especially to the New Jersey Education Association. It is time to send a strong message.
Fact is we all want great public schools and we’re all willing to invest in them. I care about that and so do you. And just so you know about my opponent who claims to be a friend of public education, there are 200 failing schools in the state as we speak, and when she was asked about that she said, “That's not a bad percentage.” Well let me tell you that is the noise coming out of the mouth of woman who's never had to send one of her children to one of those failing schools. Well when you become governor you realize
that all of these children are my children and I've got to care about their education.
Now, with three days left, we know the job ahead of us. We know the job ahead of us is to make sure that we get this vote out. And if we get this vote out, remember this, America is going to be watching New Jersey. The entire country. Our party, dispirited by the last election, dispirited by the dysfunctional craziness going on down to Washington DC by both parties, a party that is dispirited across the country. A belief is being sold by the mainstream media that we can't win anymore. Well we’ll tell them to watch New Jersey on Tuesday and watch the Republican party win again.
Now remember, we are minority party in this state. That’s not a statement of pessimism, that's a statement of fact. 750,000 more Democrats but  watch what we're going to do on Tuesday night. On Tuesday night at all of our Republicans are going to be coming out to vote. On Tuesday night, we're going to be getting a huge share of the independent vote in the state. And guess what. On Tuesday night I bet I’m going to get at least a third of the democrats in the state to vote for us because they want common sense again. That’s what is going to happen. America is going to see on Tuesday night that if you govern with strong common sense conservative principles, if you don't believe that compromise is a dirty word, if you believe that you can bring people together and work together to advance the interests of all the people of the state, they're going to see on Tuesday night that all those folks are voting together. And then we're going to have an enormous victory.
So, it’s up to us. Never forget this is a once-in-a-generation opportunity, a once-in-a-generation opportunity for our minority party. We don't get a chance every four years to do this, but this is the time we have the chance. People are listening to us and they’ve watched our performance. It’s not just about words. It's about deeds. They've watched what we’ve done. They know we inherited a broken and dispirited state that felt like it couldn't do anything right anymore and didn't even like itself when we took over. And four years later, we're back to fiscal responsibility. We're back to growing private sector jobs. We're back to lower regulation and lower taxes for our businesses. And we are back to a time once again where people are in charge of the government and not the other way around.
And as we watch this happen we've drawn more and more people to our cause. That's the way you have a successful political movement. Remember I told the Republican National Committee this August when they asked me to come speak, they said to me, “Governor, what's the secret?” I said, “We're about winning elections.” This is about winning elections. You know political parties are not debating societies everybody. They're not colleges or universities where we have a debate and the free flow of ideas towards no end. That's fine for a university, but not for a government. We're hired to do a job by you. We're paid to do a job by you. And what we need to do now is to finish that job. And we can do it the right way if we continue to work together on all the goals that we have. And now what we can do with all of these folks from this section of the state and from at the shore, for the people on the Delaware River down south and for the people who are all the way down at the Delaware Bay. What they’re all saying is, “Man oh man, government is finally working again, and I am proud to live in New Jersey.” Proud that we don’t have corruption anymore. Proud that we don’t have to worry about our government anymore.
Now there will always be the voices of dissent and you know you’ve my opponent and that's been the angriest campaign I've ever seen. I don't think there's been a day in the last hundred days that Barbara Buono hasn’t been angry about something. And her supporters deserve better than that. See campaigns based on anger never win. Campaigns are never about yesterday, they're always about tomorrow. Ad if you're angry about tomorrow nobody wants to vote for you. You have to be hopeful for tomorrow and optimistic and have a plan for tomorrow. And what the voters of New Jersey have decided is that we're the hopeful party. We're the optimistic party. We're the party with the common-sense plan for tomorrow and that's why those voices of anger can continue to yell, but we are the ones who are going to win and govern.
So just to show you that I am not asking you to do something I won’t do, I got on that bus on Wednesday and I've been on that bus since Wednesday. And I think it's Sunday, right? Because in bus years, I don’t know how long I’ve been on the bus, but it’s a long time. And so, between me and the Lieutenant Governor, we are going to make 92 stops in the last six days of this campaign. We are going to get to every county in New Jersey. Both of us are going to get to every county in this state, every legislative district in the state, campaign with every Republican legislative candidate that wants to come and campaign with us. And we are going to work as hard as we can right up until one o'clock on Election Day. They they’re going to make me go home and take a nap. But until one o’clock on Election Day I'm working. So, I need you work with me too. I need you to be there for me and for the lieutenant governor. We're going to continue to be there for you.
Sussex county was wonderful to me in 2009. I know you're going to be even better to me in 2013. We have great things still to accomplish for this state and with all of us together, all of us using our common sense, all of us using our faith in each other and our families we’ll be able to continue to make this state what it belongs: the greatest state in the United States of America. Thank you all for coming, I appreciate it.

I'm here though today to talk about the state of education in the city of Newark, and this story of education in this city is a story 20 years in the waiting. Most people say something is 20, or 30, or 40 years in the making. This is 20 years in the waiting. And it's a story that's contributed to by many people. A story, which the Newark children of today and I pray tomorrow will benefit from every day. As Governor, I need to speak the truth on these issues, both the accomplishments and the challenges to the parents of the city, to the students of the city, and to the taxpayers of this city, and the taxpayers all across the state of New Jersey, who contribute so mightily to the cost of education, K to 12 in this city. In the last six years the accomplishments of this system are very, very impressive. The job is certainly not complete. But we've made real progress at times in the face of real emotional opposition. That's why, after more than 20 years of state control, the progress made over the last six and a half years will afford the state the opportunity to return the Newark Public Schools to local control. This is a watershed moment for Newark's education community, and the work has been done by the leaders like Chris Cerf and Dave Hespy, leaders like Commissioner, Kim Harrington and Secretary Rochelle Hendricks, leaders like Mayor Baraka and Cammie Anderson, leaders like those who have served in the Newark education success board, along with the community of teachers, the parents, advocates, and the students themselves. It's been a team effort which has brought us this opportunity today.
That team effort was catapulted by the investment made by Mark Zuckerberg, Priscilla Chan, and all those who matched their $100 million investment in the Newark Public Schools. While a vocal few have profited from demeaning the importance of that investment, those of us who have been involved in this know better. The attention that that investment of their time, their voices and their money brought to the efforts spearheaded by this administration, and by then Mayor Booker, were indispensable. The achievements we outline today are due in some large measure to the belief that Mark, Priscilla, and others placed in our reform agenda. and the belief that they placed in the children of the city of Newark.
The current state of education this city can be summed up simply. Kids in Newark are getting a better education today in the Newark public schools than they did six years ago. That is undeniable. And it's improving every year. But that upward momentum can and will be lost unless we put aside old orthodoxy and we act based on the facts that are before us, not the emotion. See sometimes old entrenched failed positions can easily tear apart new partnerships in Newark that are the force behind reform, and the very reason that return of local control is even possible. While a counterproductive debate about traditional public schools versus public charter schools is still being had by those looking to settle some old scores, the schools themselves are quietly at the very same time working together in new and unprecedented ways to help the kids in Newark achieve academic success. And isn't that what matters most, our children's academic success?
So, let's finally put to rest some of the old myths about this topic, and take notice of what's happening on the ground here in this city, things that we should be very proud of. Instead of students falling further and further behind, students are in fact climbing higher and higher. In some cases, Newark students are at the top of New Jersey's class, exceeding their peers and academic accomplishment across the entire state, urban, suburban and rural. We have yet to have each and every Newark child reaching their full academic potential, and that is not only our goal, that's our moral commitment. So, let's see how far we've come since 2011. When this administration launched a broad platform of education reforms, which some vocally resisted, but have since been proven successful on the measures that count the most.
I want you all to remember that the very first visit I made as governor elect the day after the election, nearly eight years ago, was to a charter school here in Newark. Since then, in this city we have opened new schools together. We've rehabilitated old schools together. We've joined in celebrating the district's growth. We've touted success stories of individual teachers of schools, and of the students who attend those schools. So first, let's dispel some of these myths about the face of public education in Newark. There was a focus by some on the governance of the schools, more so at times than their performance. Concerns have been voiced about traditional public schools versus public charter schools, claims of competition for resources, charges of racial and economic disparities. All those claims and charges are wrong. And they are demonstrably wrong.
So, let's get a clear picture the district. Charters are not taking resources from traditional public schools. The state provides a large amount of the funding per child here in Newark. However, if a child attends a public charter school, only a portion of that funding follows the child. Public charter schools are funded less than traditional public schools and always have been. And unlike traditional public schools, they also must provide their own buildings, mostly through private fundraising. All this is done so that a portion of the funding stays with the district to cover their fixed costs that remain, even though those students have departed. Any claim to the contrary is simply untrue and motivated by desire to take this option off the menu for the parents of Newark and their children. Regarding economic and racial disparities, Newark charter schools have virtually eliminated the achievement gap for economically disadvantaged students. I want you to hear that again. Charter schools in this state have virtually eliminated the achievement gap, based upon free or reduced-price lunch membership. Charter schools in this city are attended by nearly 50% of all the African American students in Newark. 50% of the kids who are African American in this city now attend charter schools, K through 12. Our reforms have created, not just public charter schools versus traditional public schools, but a diverse portfolio of schools to better serve the diverse needs of Newark’s children. So yeah, we have traditional public schools and we have public charter schools. We also have one of the best magnet school systems in the state here in Newark. We also have the highest quality county vocational technical schools, and we've invested significant capital resources with the county to make that so. And a successful early childhood program operated in equal measure by the district's Headstart program, and by private nonprofit providers. So from Headstart, from preschool, all the way through to graduation, a diverse portfolio to give choice to the families of Newark, not based about how much money they have in their pocket but based upon what they believe is best for their child to reach their goals in life.
Good traditional public schools have opened, and poor performing ones have been closed. Good public charter schools have been open and poor performing charter schools have been closed by this administration more than by any other administration in state history. See, I don't really care about governance. I care about provable performance, documented achievement, about dreams realized, not dreams dashed. What matters is not how a public school came into being. I don't care who runs it, and under what rules. If a school is successful, the child will be successful. If that happens, everyone wins: the children, the parents, our city, the state, and our country. What really matters is where the district is improving, whether with every single year, a higher percentage of Newark’s children have access to a free quality public education, and the quality is demonstrated in the eyes of each one of those children.
Now by that standard. The work over the last six years has been a tremendous success. When we launched our reform agenda in 2011 if there was agreement about anything in Newark, it was at the schools were still in crisis. What are the foundational pieces of our children's education? Math and English. They form the basis of achievement and understanding for everything else we do. So, let's look at the numbers in 2011, Newark was in the 41st percentile in math statewide. Six years later, after these reforms Newark is now in the 75th percentile statewide for 41st to 75th in math. In 2011. Newark was in the 44th percentile in English. Six years later, Newark is now in the 78th percentile in English statewide. These are undeniable numbers, representing extraordinary achievement by Newark's children under our reforms. Next, we are meaningfully moving our children toward a diploma that matters and represents what it's supposed to represent. First we begin by making graduation real. No more social, meaningless graduation, which was happening here six years ago much too often.
How are we doing, under this new standard? In the 17 years before the reforms, the graduation rate increased by only six percentage points in 17 years. Our new reform agenda has produced demonstrable results for our families, by giving more children a diploma that means what it says. We've done this in part by having a relentless focus on improving teacher quality. Using improved tenure laws and groundbreaking new teacher contract spearheaded by this administration, Newark public schools raised the level of teacher talent in schools. A nation leading collective bargaining agreement with Newark teachers provided among other things that raises were not automatic with the passage of time but were only rewarded the teachers who were evaluated as effective. Imagine that, that your raise is based upon how you perform. And not just based upon you getting older. Today's my birthday. I got older today. I didn't get a raise. I shouldn't. Raises should be based upon performance, not just on getting older, because sometimes getting older isn't getting better. We hope it is, but sometimes it isn't. It seems basic, but it is in fact in the educational community revolutionary. It's brought revolutionary results in assuring teacher quality. In contrast to most of the rest of the country, the evaluation system did in fact differentiate performance. 14% of teachers were rated ineffective or only partially effective in 2014. That's groundbreaking, believe me. Go to other districts and see whether they are that honest about their evaluation of their teachers.
It’s long overdue that we tell parents, and all the taxpayers who are paying for this, what they're paying for, and the quality of what they're receiving in return. The continued focus on ensuring that only quality teachers remain in the classroom has led to the better retention of those teachers, and the removal of ineffective ones. So, in 2011, as I mentioned, the graduation rate was 59%, up only six points in the 17 years preceding it. That's brutally unacceptable for Newark families, for 59% graduation rate. Six years later under our reforms and stricter graduation requirements, graduation rates are now at 75%, a 16-point increase in six years. Again, the facts don't lie on deniable progress under our reforms.
We believe that Newark students need good teachers in the classroom, and they need poor teachers out of the classroom. To do that, we must use challenges to the tenure system to ensure quality. But all of you know that that was taboo before these reforms. You did not bring tenure charges against a poor performing teacher, no matter how poorly they were performing. So, what do the numbers tell us? Since we instituted these reforms. Since 2012, nearly 230 tenure charges were filed by the Newark Public Schools against poor performing teachers. Almost all those were based on effectiveness and three quarters of those resulted in teachers leaving the Newark school system. In the prior decade, 2001 to 2011, before we said teacher quality is a fundamental right of every family in Newark, do you know how many 10-year actions were filed in 10 years? 10 in 10 years. You can change what's acceptable in a classroom, but you got to fight for it.
We have fought for these reforms and kids are performing better. Why? Well, one of the reasons is because they got better teachers in front of the classrooms and they are no longer universally saddled with bad ones. And when we find bad ones we move to remove them and suggest that another profession might serve them better. Seek as you can't rid classrooms of ineffective teachers if you don't even try to rid classrooms of ineffective teachers. And here's the other effect that that has, the more effective teachers are uplifted by the removal of the less effective teachers and they remain in the district longer. The American Institute for Research did a study of this in Newark and confirmed that 95% of effective and highly effective teachers chose to remain in Newark, while only 61% of the lower rated teachers remained.
We are creating a culture in the City of Newark public schools, which says if you are good we want you we want to keep you. And if you are ineffective we want you to move on and not damage our children. And, contrary to the typical union talking points, the study shows the teachers are satisfied with the new evaluation system because they knew who was good and who wasn't without an evaluation system. Now they're happy that it's being acknowledged, both in their pay and in who is teaching those children in each classroom. Better teachers, better classrooms for Newark’s children, and better outcomes for Newark families.
The reforms brought better access to better schools with Newark’s centralized enrollment process called Newark Enrolls, parents are taking advantage of a one stop system that provides district wide options. Choosing a school that best fits their child's needs. More than half the participants selected a school that was not in their neighborhood, showing that the system is working as an intended to work. 42% of universal enrollment participants also put charters as their first choice. Choice being a powerful parental tool to ensure a student's success. Choice shouldn't be determined by economic wherewithal. Choice should be available to every parent, whether you live in Newark, or you live in Alpine. The number of charter schools in Newark has more than doubled. And the number of approved seats in charter schools in Newark has tripled. In the school year 2009-2010 when we entered office, there were eight charter schools operating in Newark approved to serve 6600 students. This school year, 17-18, eight years later, there are 19 charter schools operating in Newark approved to serve 20,500 students. While 11 charter schools have opened in Newark, just as importantly, six low performing charter schools in Newark, have been closed by this administration. Charter schools now serve almost a third of all of Newark public school students. Magnet public schools are performing even higher than charter schools, and nearly 36% of the families of Newark’s high school children have selected magnet schools for them to go to high school. They selected them because they believe this is what's best for their child. Magnet schools not only empower the children that they're educating, they empower the parents would be able to make a choice to put that child's future.
Let's talk for a moment about the Quitman School as an example of providing better access to a better school. Quitman Street Community School was once viewed as one of the most ineffective schools in the city of Newark and was identified as a renew School in 2012 under our reforms, for being one of Newark's most in need of improvement. As a renew school under the reform agenda, Quitman School leaders were required to reapply for their jobs and then had to rehire staff. They had to work for extended hours and more flexible scheduling. What's happened because of these reforms? Now the school is one of Newark’s fastest improving schools. It was recently listed number 19 of 100 schools in the nation was visiting according to Getting Smart, an online education forum. The schools that made that list achieve extraordinary results, create powerful learning, and have creative, innovative technology blends. Imagine that. Six years ago, Quitman School was so bad that all the staff and teachers were asked to reapply for their jobs. Six years later, they've gone from the bottom to the top of the game here in Newark.
This improvement would not be possible if our administration did not force change, forcing employees to keep their jobs based on quality, not years of mediocre service, which did not serve the children of that school. In our successful public charter schools, this demand for quality is showing results in dealing with New Jersey's persistent achievement gap. Newark charter schools have virtually eliminated that gap for economically disadvantaged students. In 2015-16, across New Jersey, proficiency rates for students eligible for free or reduced-price lunch trailed those for non-eligible students by 30 points in both English and Math. What are those numbers in Newark's charter schools? A three-point gap in English, and only a two-point gap in Math, between free and reduced lunch, students, and non-eligible students. Extraordinary change.
And we need to apply the success of these public charter schools to all economically disadvantaged children across the state of New Jersey, which is part of why we put charter schools in place in the first place. Operate under different rules, learn lessons from those different rules, and apply them to the rest of schools. We've done the first part, we still haven't done the second part, and economically disadvantaged children outside of Newark need to learn the lessons of what we've learned here inside Newark’s charter school experiment. Stanford's credo study found that Newark public charters generate seven months of additional learning per year in both Math and English language arts, making Newark public charter schools the second highest performing charter sector in the entire country. Seven months more of learning time.
Let's take for example North Star Academy, which is one of the highest performing schools, not in Newark, in the state. In 2016, 79% of students at NorthStar met or exceeded expectations in English Language Arts on the Park exam, placing the school in the 96th percentile statewide. In Math 69% of the students met or exceeded expectations, placing NorthStar in the 98th percentile statewide. That's incredible. And North Star Academy deserves congratulations, we're very proud of the work they're doing there. Of course, all these successful schools are made up of some outstanding students. Let's take a moment and put some faces behind the success.
One of those students is Genesis Canella from American History High School, who enrolled in honors courses freshman year and by senior year learned to balance a course load that included both AP classes and Essex County college courses. Genesis couldn't join us today because she's in class, but her sister and her aunt have joined us. And I want to extend welcome to them. Genesis was the captain the debate team, junior cheerleading coach, and a Rutgers future scholar. She participated in volleyball, softball, and the science club as well. Genesis is attending Davidson College this year, and they are very lucky to have one of Newark’s stars now at Davidson. An amazing story of an amazing student reaching her potential in Newark's public school system.
We've collaborated on many of these reforms and we have forced others. We've negotiated some as well. In six years, this is what we've seen: four-year graduation rates are up, academic proficiency is up, college enrollment is up. Hard-earned the achievement by these children, because we put them first and politics was put behind.
In 2017 75% of Newark public school graduates are attending two- and four-year colleges. 75% of those who graduate are going to two- and four-year colleges. Students have been accepted to 135 different technical, community, and four-year colleges across the country. Several Newark charter schools have achieved over 90% matriculation of students to college. This year seven students from Newark will be attending Ivy League universities on full scholarships to Yale, to Princeton, Penn and Harvard. As part of the school reforms, the city of Newark is now tracking student’s success more aggressively and, as a result, providing proper counseling services and resources to help students increase access to available scholarship opportunities to make college real for them in an affordable way. As a result, in 2017 students from the Newark Public Schools have received more than $15.7 million in scholarships.
There's another amazing personal story to the city-wide success: valedictorian of her class at Malcolm X Shabazz High School, Kim Borger is attending Harvard University this fall, where she hopes to feed her love of science. Malcolm X Shabazz is a comprehensive high school in Newark’s south ward. There are approximately 600 students. 90% of them qualify for free and reduced lunch program. Last year, Kim raised $6,000, with help from her teacher Patrick Murphy, and the Newark community to attend the Global Science Conference in San Francisco, with a team of students from Shabazz. The team presented their biochemical data on primary enzyme research. I had to go over that slowly because I have no idea what that is, but it sounds extraordinarily impressive. In a quote from a recent news article about Kim's achievements. She said about the fundraising effort the following, “Once it hit me that the whole literally the whole city was coming together over this, I thought it was really the most wonderful thing. Usually the only time the whole neighborhood comes together is for a candlelight vigil at Penn Station when God forbid something bad happens. But now that I could be the reason for the whole neighborhood coming together. It's a good thing. My heart skipped a beat.” For Kim we wish her a successful first semester at Harvard. Newark and the whole state of New Jersey are cheering for her and what she represents about what's so good about the city, and about our state.
And her recognition of how powerful it can be when the whole neighborhood comes together is the same power we're seeing when Newark’s broader education community comes together, rather than fighting each other. Going through reform process is difficult in any operation. It's particularly hard when you transform a school system that has long been part of the city's cultural history, in addition to its educational history. So, reweaving the very fabric of the school system in Newark is always going to have its challenges and there always be those who will oppose change, either because they're in denial of the failure around them, or because the old system benefits them personally.
But we've had a couple of very tough visionary leaders in this city, who have refused to accept the status quo. Chris Cerf and Cami Andersen, they've refused to accept the failure. That was around us six years ago and so have I. And what evolves when those reforms are producing good results, in this case, giving our kids a better education, is a momentum that starts a blending of the best of the new and the old that raises the bar. Let me assure you, the Newark public education system is rising. The statistics cannot be denied. The results shout for continued reform for Newark’s children, and it's on us, the leaders and parents of the city and the state, to keep the momentum going. We carry both that burden and that privilege. We must work together in the interest of Newark’s families. They deserve nothing less than that. One example is a recent collaboration between the Newark Public Schools and the uncommon public charter schools where they're working together to increase student resources and support for the students. A program called Great Habits, Great Readers provides professional development for educators to ensure more targeted and specific summer reading instruction for rising second graders who are not yet reading at grade level. So, with the help of uncommon school staff members, these educators are receiving increased training and development and practical strategies they can use to help the students learn better reading habits. The training is a continuation of an ongoing collaborative relationship between the Newark public schools and uncommon schools in the area of literacy.
Over the last two years the organizations have opened classrooms and schools to each other. They shared resources in order to learn from each other's practices for the benefit of the students here in Newark. Enrollment in the summer program is free and it increased by 50% compared to last year with 750 students enrolling for the 2017 summer program. Uncommon is also partnering with Newark to provide professional development for both teachers and administrators. Uncommon schools piloted this year a leader to leader mentoring program with a select group of Newark public school principals. In 2014, North Star Academy and Uncommon embarked upon a turnaround of the Alexander Street Elementary School, a place I went and visited myself. Born out of a partnership with the Newark public schools, the school is seeing remarkable results with a cohort of students who once struggled under different leadership. These students have performed exceedingly well in the 2015 Park exams. Fourth graders boasted proficiency rates of 60% in English and 70% in math, beating the state averages of 51% and 40% respectively. Scores further increased in 2016 with 70% of Alexander street third and fourth graders proficient in English and 75% of the third and fourth graders proficient math. Prior to this collaboration Alexander street school was failing and was marked for closure. And as a result, the children who were going there were failing. Pride should never be placed ahead of progress. At Alexander street school, we put the children first and as a result, they are now achieving great things as they move to the next stage of their education.
Marion P Thomas charter school is developing a Hospitality and Culinary Arts program for its high school students. That'll create a unique opportunity for students to develop skills that will translate to the workforce, if that's where they choose to go. In 2014 Newark public schools Office of expanded learning time partnered with the statewide after school network and used grant funding to provide technical assistance and professional development, data collection and evaluation to all district after school and summer programs. And what's that reform and partnership done for Newark students? The summer Plus Program is a district wide initiative to curb summer learning loss. This program summer plus combines academic programs and cultural enrichment into a full day program. Summer plus has been developed by Newark public school’s curriculum experts to improve critical math and literacy skills and ensure that participants are well prepared to start school in September. And it's open to students’ grades K through 7.
I also want to recognize today the extraordinary teachers across this district who share the same goal to help children reach their greatest potential. Two teachers deserve specific mention today. One who comes from a long line of educators and teachers in a traditional Newark public school and one who teaches in Newark Public Charter School. They work under different governance structures, but more importantly, they work under one shared goal.
First let me welcome Whitney Frond, who was the Newark teacher of the year two years ago. She's a middle school math teacher, and debate coach at Mount Vernon school. In 2016, when she was chosen out of 30 finalists, as Teacher of the Year, her students significantly outperformed not only the district averages, but the state averages as well. She also dedicates her own time after school each week, to ensure her students are able to participate in extracurricular activities like the Mount Vernon debate team, which is ranked as one of the top teams in all the Newark public schools, at least in part as a result to her leadership. In fact, one of her protegees, Brianna Aaron, is a nationally renowned champion debater who attend Science Park here in the city. Miss Frond began her teaching at Mount Vernon nine years ago as part of a family tradition. The father founded what is now Newark Debate Academy, and her mother was an educator and school administrator. We need to thank her for her decade of service at Mount Vernon, and even more for a dedication that she shares both inside and outside the classroom with her students.
Let me now welcome Mr. Christopher Velazquez. He's a sixth-grade math teacher and a co grade level leader at Great Oaks Legacy charter school. He was raised in the Bronx and had the good fortune to come across two teachers during his high school career that helped shape the trajectory of his life. They inspired him, they supported him, and they challenged him,  one in an AP English classroom and one on the baseball field. But both nonetheless made a lasting impact. Thanks to their investment in him, Mr. Velazquez knew he wanted to pursue teaching to be able to educate and inspire other students. After graduating from Hunter College, Mr. Vasquez joined Great Oak Legacies tutor corps program, a year of service that focuses on providing individualized education to urban students. He quickly proved that he had both the skills and the gifts to succeed as a teacher and a leader, and that he would now begin to help shape Newark’s future leaders. Great Oaks is a high performing tier one charter school. It was approved to open in 2011. In 2016, it consolidated with Newark legacy and became Great Oaks Legacy. Great Oaks Legacy is now a K-12 school approved to serve 1906 students in this school year. The school's ability to develop talent is impressive. In 2015-16 median student growth among middle schoolers was 82 in math, which is better than 98.9% of all public schools serving any or all grades six to eight in the state.
Additionally, the school recruits, houses, and trains a tutor corps, which provides every middle and high school student at Great Oaks Legacy with two hours of tutoring daily during the school year. During his first two years of great oaks legacy, Mr. Velazquez tutored some of the most challenging students and helped motivate them to stay in school. He also began mentoring his fellow teachers on how to be more effective in their roles. His third year great Oaks, he joined Relay Graduate School of Education, in order to obtain his masters and was offered a teaching position and had probably the best first year someone could have. Mr. Velazquez accomplished a difficult task by striking the right balance between relating to and building connections with students, but also maintaining high expectations and academic rigor. Now in his second year of teaching and assuming responsibility of co-grade level leader, we will undoubtedly be hearing more of Mr. Velazquez in the future.
Its efforts like his and Ms. Frond’s that brought us here today and he deserves our thanks as well.
So, let's talk about the promising future of the Newark public schools. I’ve spent a lot of time talking about the last six years. Next week on September 13, the State Board of Education with my support and encouragement is expected to approve returning the last two areas of state control governance and instructional program to local control of the people of city of Newark. Newark Public Schools has demonstrated substantial progress in these areas, and it is evidenced that the school district has the programs, the policies, and the personnel in place to ensure that the progress will be sustained. Through collaboration between district leadership, and the Newark public schools Board of Education, the district's budget is now better aligned to the district's instructional goals and the needs of the students. And I want to tell you that that would not have happened without the leadership of Superintendent Cerf
Newark’s public schools now have higher graduation rates, better schools with better access, better teachers, and increased academic proficiency. But we must stay focused on our efforts. Recognizing the success of our reforms but also being aware of the improvements that are still needed. As part of handing over local control, the board will pass a resolution triggering the creation of a transition plan. That transition plan must set priorities and benchmarks in areas of academics and students supports, teacher professional development, community engagement, and efficient governance. Newark public schools owes much of its success to a collaborative effort between the district, the Department of Education, local government and community leaders. The district has worked diligently. It has implemented this tough reform agenda to look at the various school options with different governance structures as partners, not as competitors, not as adversaries, not as enemies. There are always going to be special interests who want to keep fueling an unproductive and dishonest point of view that will recreate division and acrimony. That doesn't benefit the students, or their families and we should not permit them to reemerge.
The facts behind nurse improvement are undeniable in the last six years and the only variable is the reform agenda that this administration for every day. There's still plenty of room for improvement, especially in our core areas. We need to address the district's chronic absenteeism rate, which at 30% will remain a significant barrier to long term student success. English language arts and math proficiency rates have shown real progress, but are still below where they need to be for the children in Newark and district proficiency rates on Park, even with a dramatic improvement in the first two years of testing, are still more than 20 percentage points below the state average. So, we must remain vigilant and present in maintaining the upward momentum we've achieved through our reforms, because we must go farther on behalf of the students and the parents that we serve.
We cannot crawl towards the 13 points we need to add to our four-year graduation rate in order to catch up to the state average. Under the old education model, prior to our reforms, it would take 30 years to close that gap. I don't think any of us are willing to accept that slow a pace of progress. Too many children will get lost if we go back to the old ways of one size fits all governance and allowing teacher tenure, to protect poor performing educators.
And we haven't discussed politics today. We have not because getting politics out of this process is what led to these reforms being adopted and these results being achieved by Newark students. There is, however, a disturbing breeze blowing in the political world on education. Quiet conversations of charter school moratoriums, reversal of tenure reforms, and return to business as usual. This quiet conversation is being pushed by the same old special interest on pliable potential leaders in the mode of desperate search for votes on election day. I beg the people of Newark to repel such conversation, and to stand up for your right to choose. Don't turn that right over to special interest groups or fast-talking hucksters begging for your vote.
Stand up for your kids. They need you now. As we hand over the reins back to local control, I offer nothing but support and hope for the success of this endeavor. But I also want to emphasize again, that holding our children's future in our hands as leaders is both an awesome responsibility and a great privilege. We as leaders, as parents, as community advocates, and as teachers are the best hope for helping these kids obtain a better future.
I was born in Newark and I lived here for the first five years of my life. My mom and dad, who were lifelong Newarkers, left for one reason and one reason only. They were worried that the Newark Public Schools would not provide for their children what the Newark public schools had provided for them. Those who could leave often did. Those who could not or chose not to leave were left with a broken failing school system that, 20 years ago, left the state with no choice but to take over the district from local control. I'm proud today to be their son. They left Newark, the home they loved and the only home they ever knew, because they wanted more for me. How proud my mother would be, and my father is to watch their son spend six years fighting for the school system that educated them. How proud they are that it is their son, a native Newarker too, who's the governor who fought the special interests, who helped bring Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan to Newark, who negotiated to reward good teachers and fire bad ones, and to get parents, just like them the power to choose the best school for their child. And my parents had no such choice. Their only choice was binary: stay or go.
They're proud of all the improvements Newark children have shown. I know that my mom, would be so happy that it was her son, who turned the Newark schools back to the families of Newark, and out of state control better than I found it. Let the facts about Newark students’ academic success be your greatest guide as we move forward. That is all that truly matters in helping them achieve their dreams. It has been an honor and a privilege to be a governor who has worked so closely with the city and its community to give our children a better future. And I hope and pray that all of you who are as committed to this cause today will remain that committed. And we'll give each and every family in this city the opportunity to choose the best path for their child, and then help those families achieve their dreams and their goals. When that occurs then we will have gotten everywhere we need to on Newark. We've come a very long way in six years. I'm proud to have been a small part of it. And I'm very happy to call the Newark public school system partners in this change and in this growth. Thank you all for coming.
